title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for Long-Horizon Multimodal Search Agents

paper.title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for Long-Horizon Multimodal Search Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multimodal deep search is moving from short queries to long-horizon
investigations that continually acquire evidence. However, training
such agents remains constrained by limited challenging training
questions and insufficient process feedback.
We introduce MMSearch-OPD , combining controllable data
refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy
distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline performs targeted
expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple
multimodal questions. Parameterized transformations control
search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing
existing image–question pairs. For training, answer rewards and
lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap
modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect student
trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient
reduces teacher dependence as training proceeds.
Experiments show gains from data refinement and further
improvements from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger
long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Motivation for MMSearch-OPD and an example of Refine for long-horizon multimodal search. Multimodal deep search agents address knowledge-intensive visual questions through interleaved reasoning and external retrieval ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Recent advances move toward long-horizon investigation, connecting evidence across webpages and using acquired visual observations to guide subsequent searches ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Two challenges limit training for this setting. Existing multimodal datasets contain many questions solvable through parametric knowledge or short retrieval, while constructing harder questions through graph composition and visual enrichment entails relation collection, image curation, and evidence validation ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Reusing existing image–question pairs offers a starting point for constructing questions with greater search demands. Meanwhile, useful long-horizon investigation may end in redundant verification, premature stopping, or an incorrect answer. Terminal rewards provide limited process feedback, and trajectory-level advantages supply a shared scalar signal throughout a rollout ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Identical returns also remove group-relative learning contrast. Process rewards and teacher guidance address these limitations ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) ; we combine outcome-based optimization with selective token-level teacher guidance. To address these challenges, we propose MMSearch-OPD , combining controllable question refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline reuses simple multimodal questions and their candidate reasoning chains. Expand extends chain depth, Blur increases disambiguation requirements, and Visualize introduces retrievable visual evidence. These configurable operators control the intended evidence requirements while reusing seed assets (Figure 1 ). After question validation and supervised initialization, joint training combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with token-level OPD on imperfect student trajectories. The shaped reward gap adjusts guidance strength, while an exponential schedule reduces the OPD coefficient as training proceeds. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce Refine, a pipeline that reuses existing multimodal questions and adjusts their evidence requirements through chain expansion, entity disambiguation, and visual evidence requirements. • We develop joint RL and selective OPD training that combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-gap-weighted token guidance and exponential annealing on imperfect long-horizon search trajectories. • We organize evaluation across ten multimodal search benchmarks to assess agent performance and the roles of data refinement and joint training.

sections.heading: Long-Horizon Multimodal Search.
sections.text: MMSearch-R1 and WebWatcher train multimodal agents to interleave reasoning with external retrieval ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Recent work extends search horizons and manages growing interaction histories ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . DeepVoyager-VL uses intermediate visual evidence to guide subsequent search ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These developments call for training questions requiring sustained, cross-modal evidence acquisition.

sections.heading: Multimodal Search Data Construction.
sections.text: Questions solvable through parametric knowledge or short retrieval provide limited supervision for long-horizon search. Existing pipelines increase difficulty through multi-hop composition and entity obfuscation ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , graph-structured synthesis ( Chu et al., 2026 ; Mei et al., 2026 ) , and visual evidence integration ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These constructions require evidence collection and validation. Our Refine pipeline reuses existing easy questions and candidate reasoning chains, applying Expand, Blur, and Visualize to control chain length, disambiguation, and visual requirements without building a large graph from scratch.

sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Search.
sections.text: GRPO-based training improves search policies through interaction ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , but terminal scores offer limited feedback on partially useful trajectories. Process rewards, adaptive sampling, and finer credit assignment address this limitation ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Dai et al., 2026 ; Jiao et al., 2026 ; Mei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . HyperEyes combines efficiency rewards with teacher distillation on failed rollouts ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Our joint optimization combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-gap-weighted teacher guidance on imperfect student trajectories, using exponential annealing to reduce reliance on the SFT teacher during training. sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: MMSearch-OPD combines controllable question refinement with joint RL–OPD training. Refine increases textual and visual evidence requirements; after validation and supervised initialization, outcome rewards and behavior penalties guide RL, while selective, reward-gap-weighted token guidance supports learning on imperfect student trajectories.

sections.heading: Long-horizon multimodal search.
sections.text: Given a question–image pair x = ( q , ℐ ) x=(q,\mathcal{I}) , an agent π θ \pi_{\theta} interleaves reasoning with web search and image inspection until returning an answer. Later actions depend on the accumulated multimodal history h t h_{t} , making evidence acquisition sequential. For example, identifying an entity in a retrieved image can determine the next textual query; facts found on a webpage can instead guide which image to inspect.

sections.heading: Seed collection.
sections.text: We take the full training splits of LiveVQA and FVQA and retain questions that the data-generation model answers correctly without tools. These seeds are easy for this model, and their successful chain-of-thought provides candidate reasoning chains.

Expand increases chain depth, Blur introduces entity disambiguation, and Visualize adds retrieved visual evidence. The operators modify the designated chain before question wording is synthesized, allowing their evidence requirements to be controlled separately.

sections.heading: Question validation.
sections.text: Each synthesized question is walked through from the input image, with minimal wording fixes to ensure solvability and answer uniqueness. We check chain consistency, evidence provenance, image–text alignment, and actual use of the designated Blur and Visualize evidence. These checks approximate Equation 1 and help ensure that the added requirements in Equation 8 are non-trivial.

sections.heading: Difficulty filtering and trajectory selection.
sections.text: We discard questions answered correctly by a direct-answer probe without tools. An expert model then performs k k tool-augmented rollouts per question using the training search-and-vision interface. The probe removes residual parametric shortcuts that refinement alone cannot rule out, while tool-augmented rollouts test whether the questions are learnable through external evidence acquisition. The expert’s empirical Pass@ k k measures agent difficulty, complementing the chain-based evidence burden D Refined D_{\mathrm{Refined}} . We retain successful trajectories as SFT demonstrations, sampling across Pass@ k k levels to balance difficulty and prevent easy questions from dominating supervision. These estimates also guide the SFT/RL split described in Section 3.4 .

sections.heading: Supervised initialization.
sections.text: Using the difficulty estimates in Section 3.3 , we partition the curated training questions into an SFT subset and a harder RL subset. A larger model is fine-tuned on successful trajectories from both subsets and frozen as teacher π T \pi_{\mathrm{T}} . The student π θ \pi_{\theta} is initialized by SFT on the first subset and jointly optimized with RL and OPD on the second.

Final-answer scores provide limited feedback on these intermediate decisions, motivating guidance along the search process. We combine outcome-based policy optimization with token-level teacher guidance on the student’s own trajectories, supplementing the shared scalar feedback from trajectory-wide advantages. For each question, we sample G G student rollouts and assign correctness scores c i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{i}\in[0,1] . sections.heading: Models and Training Data.
sections.text: We use Seed2.1-Pro ( ByteDance Seed, 2026 ) to generate SFT trajectories. Qwen3.5-27B is fine-tuned on all curated trajectories and frozen as the OPD teacher. Qwen3.5-9B receives SFT on a subset, followed by joint RL–OPD training on harder questions. We report its SFT and RL checkpoints.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate on MMSearch ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , LiveVQA ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , BrowseComp-VL ( Geng et al., 2025 ) , MM-BrowseComp ( Li et al., 2025 ) , MMSearch-Plus ( Tao et al., 2026 ) , BrowseComp-V 3 ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , and VisBrowse-Bench ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) . We use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B to judge final-answer correctness with the Vision-DeepResearch judge prompt ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Each prediction is judged three times, and the scores are averaged. Avg. is the unweighted benchmark mean.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare tool-free Direct Answer , tool-enabled Agentic Workflow , and trained Multimodal Deep Search Agents , grouping the latter by model scale.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: We use ms-swift for SFT and veRL for joint RL–OPD training. The agent interleaves reasoning with textual and visual retrieval, with a maximum of 50 interaction turns per evaluation question.

sections.heading: Overall Performance.
sections.text: Table 1 shows that MMSearch-OPD-9B reaches 60.2 average accuracy, improving over the corresponding Qwen3.5-9B agentic workflow by 15.3 points. It achieves the highest reported accuracy among the compared 7B–9B search agents on all seven benchmarks, exceeding DeepVoyager-VL-8B by 9.6 points on average. The 27B SFT teacher reaches 63.2, a 6.5-point improvement over its agentic-workflow baseline. The trained 9B student also exceeds the untuned 27B workflow by 3.5 points on average.

sections.heading: Long-Horizon Multimodal Search.
sections.text: MMSearch-OPD improves performance across the evaluated search settings, gaining 12.8 points on average over the same 9B agentic workflow on MMSearch, LiveVQA, and BrowseComp-VL. In particular, it gains 17.2 points on average on MM-BrowseComp, MMSearch-Plus, BrowseComp-V 3 , and VisBrowse-Bench, which place substantial demands on long-horizon investigation and cross-modal evidence integration. These results demonstrate substantial improvements in search settings requiring sustained evidence acquisition and joint reasoning over text and images.

sections.heading: Joint Training Beyond SFT.
sections.text: The 9B SFT checkpoint already improves average accuracy from 44.9 to 57.9. Subsequent joint RL–OPD training, labeled RL in Table 1 , further raises it to 60.2, with improvements on every benchmark. The 2.3-point average gain supports joint online optimization after SFT.

sections.heading: 4.3.2 Refine Pipeline Ablation
sections.text: We follow the same 100 seed questions through Expand, Blur, and Visualize, synthesizing a question from each intermediate structure. Seed2.1-Pro solves all four versions under identical rollout settings. Figure 5 reports accuracy, search length, and tool-use composition. Each search request within a batched action counts as one tool call. Each step strengthens the questions’ search requirements: accuracy decreases from 79% to 65%, 44%, and 33%. Expand lowers accuracy with little change in interaction length; Blur increases average turns from 10.2 to 15.1, consistent with additional entity disambiguation. Visualize further raises turns to 20.2 and tool calls to 34.7 per question, while ImageSearch and FetchImage’s combined share of tool actions increases from 6.3% to 47.5%. These results support the complementary roles of chain expansion, disambiguation, and visual evidence acquisition in constructing harder long-horizon multimodal search tasks.

sections.heading: Reward Dynamics.
sections.text: Figure 5 (a) shows mean answer reward before behavior penalties rising from 0.347 to 0.587 over 19 steps. Despite batch fluctuations, this trend indicates improved answer quality during joint RL–OPD training.

sections.heading: Search Behavior.
sections.text: Search trajectories initially lengthen and then contract (Figure 5 (b)). Comparing steps 6–13 with steps 14–19, average tool calls decrease from 26.0 to 21.3 (18.3%), and generated response length falls from 29.0k to 23.4k tokens (19.5%), while mean answer reward remains comparable (0.525 versus 0.544). These observations are consistent with increasingly economical search: later rollouts use fewer interactions and generated tokens without a corresponding decline in average answer quality. These batch-level trends describe the joint training run rather than isolate the effect of individual components.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable data refinement with joint RL–OPD training for long-horizon multimodal deep search. Refine reuses existing multimodal question–image pairs and applies targeted transformations to control search depth, entity disambiguation, and visual evidence requirements. Joint training complements answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-conditioned token-level guidance on imperfect student trajectories, while progressively reducing teacher influence. Across seven primary benchmarks, our 9B agent improves average accuracy by 15.3 percentage points over its agentic-workflow baseline, with joint training adding 2.3 points beyond SFT. Data ablations further support the training value of refined questions. Together, these results show the value of upgrading existing multimodal data to require sustained evidence acquisition. They also support joint outcome optimization and selective teacher guidance for learning long-horizon search and reasoning over text and images.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Refine increases evidence requirements along designated reasoning chains, but filtering cannot rule out all shortcuts from parametric knowledge or alternative web evidence. Training depends on teacher and answer-judge quality, which may introduce noisy guidance. Open-web search also relies on changing content and tool availability, limiting reproducibility.

However, training such agents remains constrained by limited challenging training questions and insufficient process feedback. We introduce MMSearch-OPD , combining controllable data refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline performs targeted expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple multimodal questions. Parameterized transformations control search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing existing image–question pairs. For training, answer rewards and lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect student trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient reduces teacher dependence as training proceeds. Experiments show gains from data refinement and further improvements from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Motivation for MMSearch-OPD and an example of Refine for long-horizon multimodal search. Multimodal deep search agents address knowledge-intensive visual questions through interleaved reasoning and external retrieval ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Recent advances move toward long-horizon investigation, connecting evidence across webpages and using acquired visual observations to guide subsequent searches ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Two challenges limit training for this setting. Existing multimodal datasets contain many questions solvable through parametric knowledge or short retrieval, while constructing harder questions through graph composition and visual enrichment entails relation collection, image curation, and evidence validation ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Reusing existing image–question pairs offers a starting point for constructing questions with greater search demands. Meanwhile, useful long-horizon investigation may end in redundant verification, premature stopping, or an incorrect answer. Terminal rewards provide limited process feedback, and trajectory-level advantages supply a shared scalar signal throughout a rollout ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Identical returns also remove group-relative learning contrast. Process rewards and teacher guidance address these limitations ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) ; we combine outcome-based optimization with selective token-level teacher guidance. To address these challenges, we propose MMSearch-OPD , combining controllable question refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline reuses simple multimodal questions and their candidate reasoning chains. Expand extends chain depth, Blur increases disambiguation requirements, and Visualize introduces retrievable visual evidence. These configurable operators control the intended evidence requirements while reusing seed assets (Figure 1 ). After question validation and supervised initialization, joint training combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with token-level OPD on imperfect student trajectories. The shaped reward gap adjusts guidance strength, while an exponential schedule reduces the OPD coefficient as training proceeds. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce Refine, a pipeline that reuses existing multimodal questions and adjusts their evidence requirements through chain expansion, entity disambiguation, and visual evidence requirements. • We develop joint RL and selective OPD training that combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-gap-weighted token guidance and exponential annealing on imperfect long-horizon search trajectories. • We organize evaluation across ten multimodal search benchmarks to assess agent performance and the roles of data refinement and joint training. 2 Related Work Long-Horizon Multimodal Search. MMSearch-R1 and WebWatcher train multimodal agents to interleave reasoning with external retrieval ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Recent work extends search horizons and manages growing interaction histories ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . DeepVoyager-VL uses intermediate visual evidence to guide subsequent search ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These developments call for training questions requiring sustained, cross-modal evidence acquisition. Multimodal Search Data Construction. Questions solvable through parametric knowledge or short retrieval provide limited supervision for long-horizon search. Existing pipelines increase difficulty through multi-hop composition and entity obfuscation ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , graph-structured synthesis ( Chu et al., 2026 ; Mei et al., 2026 ) , and visual evidence integration ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These constructions require evidence collection and validation. Our Refine pipeline reuses existing easy questions and candidate reasoning chains, applying Expand, Blur, and Visualize to control chain length, disambiguation, and visual requirements without building a large graph from scratch. Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Search. GRPO-based training improves search policies through interaction ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , but terminal scores offer limited feedback on partially useful trajectories. Process rewards, adaptive sampling, and finer credit assignment address this limitation ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Dai et al., 2026 ; Jiao et al., 2026 ; Mei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . HyperEyes combines efficiency rewards with teacher distillation on failed rollouts ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Our joint optimization combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-gap-weighted teacher guidance on imperfect student trajectories, using exponential annealing to reduce reliance on the SFT teacher during training. Despite batch fluctuations, this trend indicates improved answer quality during joint RL–OPD training. Search Behavior. Search trajectories initially lengthen and then contract (Figure 5 (b)). Comparing steps 6–13 with steps 14–19, average tool calls decrease from 26.0 to 21.3 (18.3%), and generated response length falls from 29.0k to 23.4k tokens (19.5%), while mean answer reward remains comparable (0.525 versus 0.544). These observations are consistent with increasingly economical search: later rollouts use fewer interactions and generated tokens without a corresponding decline in average answer quality. These batch-level trends describe the joint training run rather than isolate the effect of individual components. 5 Conclusion We introduced MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable data refinement with joint RL–OPD training for long-horizon multimodal deep search. Refine reuses existing multimodal question–image pairs and applies targeted transformations to control search depth, entity disambiguation, and visual evidence requirements. Joint training complements answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-conditioned token-level guidance on imperfect student trajectories, while progressively reducing teacher influence. Across seven primary benchmarks, our 9B agent improves average accuracy by 15.3 percentage points over its agentic-workflow baseline, with joint training adding 2.3 points beyond SFT. Data ablations further support the training value of refined questions. Together, these results show the value of upgrading existing multimodal data to require sustained evidence acquisition. They also support joint outcome optimization and selective teacher guidance for learning long-horizon search and reasoning over text and images. Limitations Refine increases evidence requirements along designated reasoning chains, but filtering cannot rule out all shortcuts from parametric knowledge or alternative web evidence. Training depends on teacher and answer-judge quality, which may introduce noisy guidance. Open-web search also relies on changing content and tool availability, limiting reproducibility.
